title: Diagnose a dead outlet with a lamp (no multimeter)
mechanism_check: Confirm the device you are testing with actually works: plug the lamp into a known-live outlet first and see it light.
Check whether the outlet is a GFCI or downstream of one (small TEST/RESET buttons) before anything else.
Look at the breaker panel for a tripped breaker: a switch sitting halfway between ON and OFF.
improvised_tools: Table lamp or phone charger as the test device instead of a multimeter
Tape and marker to label the breaker once found
Phone camera flashlight to read a dark breaker panel
steps: Plug the lamp into the dead outlet. If it stays dark, the outlet is dead (not the lamp).
Press RESET on any nearby GFCI outlet, then re-test. A tripped GFCI upstream kills everything downstream of it.
Go to the breaker panel: flip any tripped (halfway) breaker fully OFF, then fully ON.
Re-test the outlet with the lamp. If it works, note what overloaded the circuit.
If the lamp stays dark and no breaker is tripped, check whether the outlet is switch-controlled (flip nearby wall switches and re-test).
stop_conditions: Stop and call a licensed electrician if the breaker trips again immediately after reset with nothing plugged in.
Stop if you smell burning plastic, see scorch marks, or feel heat at the outlet — kill the breaker and call an electrician.
Never open the outlet or remove the cover plate yourself in this entry — that is applied-level work.

title: Strip wire cleanly without wire strippers
mechanism_check: Identify the wire type first: solid copper (stiff, single strand) versus stranded copper (bends easily). The method differs.
Note the insulation thickness: thick rubber-jacket cord needs a shallow score; thin THHN needs a single pinch.
Work de-energized always: confirm the cord is unplugged or the breaker is OFF and verified dead before touching conductor.
improvised_tools: Pocket knife, box cutter, or utility blade as the stripping edge
Fingernails or a lighter for very thin insulation on low-voltage leads
A drill bit of matching gauge as a strip-length gauge (strip no more than 1/2 inch)
steps: De-energize: unplug the cord or kill the breaker, then verify with a lamp test that power is off.
Lay the wire on a firm surface and roll the knife gently around the insulation at the strip point — score it, do not cut through.
Bend the wire at the score so the insulation cracks open, then pull the scored sleeve off.
Inspect the bare copper: it must be shiny and nick-free. Nicked copper is a future break point — re-cut and strip again.
Twist stranded conductors tight so no stray strands splay outward.
stop_conditions: Stop if the copper is nicked more than a quarter of its diameter after three attempts — cut back further or call an electrician.
Stop if insulation is melted, brittle, or crumbling along the run; the wire is heat-damaged and the circuit needs professional inspection.
Any doubt the circuit is dead: stop and verify before stripping — stripping a live wire is how injuries happen.

title: Test and reset a GFCI outlet
mechanism_check: GFCI outlets protect against ground faults by cutting power in milliseconds when current leaks to ground; the TEST button simulates that leak.
One GFCI often protects every outlet downstream of it — a dead bathroom outlet may be caused by the garage GFCI.
The RESET button only stays in when the outlet has line power; it will not reset on a dead circuit.
improvised_tools: A lamp or night-light as the test load — plug it in before pressing TEST
A hair dryer as a known heavy load to confirm the reset holds under current
steps: Plug a lamp into the GFCI outlet and confirm it is lit.
Press TEST. The lamp must go out and RESET should pop out. If it does not trip, the GFCI is failed — replace it.
Press RESET firmly until it clicks in. The lamp should relight.
If RESET will not stay in, unplug everything downstream and try once more. If it still will not hold, the GFCI or its wiring is faulty.
Test the monthly-test habit: TEST then RESET once a month on kitchen, bath, garage, and outdoor GFCIs.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if RESET trips again instantly with nothing plugged in — there is a ground fault in the wiring.
Stop if the GFCI outlet is warm, buzzing, or smells of heat; kill its breaker and call an electrician.
Never tape or wedge the RESET button in — a GFCI that will not hold is telling you something.

title: Read hot, neutral, and ground wire colors
mechanism_check: US residential convention: black or red = hot (carries power), white or gray = neutral (return path), bare copper or green = ground (safety path).
On a lamp cord, the ribbed side or white-stripe side is the neutral; the smooth side is hot. The wide prong is neutral, narrow is hot.
Convention is not proof: in old or DIY-modified houses colors may be wrong, which is why verification matters more than color.
improvised_tools: Phone camera zoomed into the box to photograph wire layout before you touch anything
Masking tape and marker to tag each wire by color and position before disconnecting
Lamp test (plug into a live outlet) to confirm the test lamp works before trusting it for verification
steps: Kill the breaker for the circuit and verify dead with a lamp plugged into the outlet or fixture box.
Open the box and photograph the wiring exactly as found — this photo is your reassembly map.
Tag each wire with tape: mark black/red as HOT, white as NEUTRAL, bare/green as GROUND.
On lamp cord, identify the ribbed/stripe side as neutral before cutting — verify by tracing to the wide prong.
Keep tags on until the device is mounted and tested; remove them only after the circuit works.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if you find knob-and-tube wiring, cloth-insulated wire, or aluminum branch wiring — all need professional handling.
Stop if colors do not match convention (e.g. white wire connected as hot without red/black re-marking tape) and you cannot trace the circuit confidently.
Stop if more than one circuit appears to share the same box and you cannot identify each feed with the breaker panel.

title: Twist a strong wire splice with wire nuts
mechanism_check: A wire nut joins conductors by biting into a pre-twisted bundle; the twist carries the current, the nut insulates and locks it.
Match nut size to wire count and gauge: a nut too small will not seat, a nut too large will spin loose.
Splices live inside boxes only — never buried in a wall without a box, and a box must stay accessible.
improvised_tools: Linesman pliers or needle-nose pliers to pre-twist when no crimp tool exists
A bottle cap or rubber glove for extra grip when twisting the nut tight
Electrical tape as a secondary wrap over the nut (never the primary joint)
steps: De-energize and verify dead. Strip 1/2 inch of insulation from each conductor.
Hold the bare ends parallel, aligned evenly, and twist them clockwise together with pliers — tight, no splaying.
Screw the wire nut on clockwise until it is snug and no bare copper shows below the skirt.
Tug each wire individually — none should move. Re-do any that slips.
Fold the splice gently into the box, nut-up, and reinstall the cover before restoring power.
stop_conditions: Stop if the nut spins freely or copper shows beneath it after re-seating — get the correct nut size or call an electrician.
Stop if you must splice aluminum to copper: that joint needs listed alumiconn connectors and antioxidant, done by an electrician.
Never splice inside a wall cavity without an accessible box; if there is no box, call an electrician to add one.

title: Replace a damaged extension cord plug end
mechanism_check: A replacement plug end clamps the cord jacket for strain relief and terminates hot/neutral/ground on brass, silver, and green screws.
Brass screw = hot (narrow prong), silver screw = neutral (wide prong), green screw = ground (round prong).
Cut the cord above the damage: damaged conductor inside the jacket hides corrosion and heat damage.
improvised_tools: Replacement plug end from a hardware store (sized to the cord gauge) — the only part you cannot improvise
Knife or scissors to cut and strip the jacket when strippers are missing
Screwdriver you already own; the plug's strain-relief bar is tightened by hand
steps: Unplug the cord. Cut off the damaged plug plus at least 2 inches of cord above the damage.
Slit the outer jacket back about 2 inches without nicking the inner conductors; strip 1/2 inch off each conductor.
Open the new plug, feed the cord through the shell, and loop each conductor clockwise under its screw: black to brass, white to silver, green to ground.
Tighten screws firmly, confirm no stray strands, then tighten the strain-relief clamp over the jacket.
Plug in and test with a lamp before using on a real load; flex the plug end while testing to catch an intermittent.
stop_conditions: Stop if the cord jacket is melted, brittle, or damaged in multiple spots — replace the whole cord.
Stop if the cord is undersized for its load (thin lamp cord on a space heater); a new plug does not make it safe.
Any cord that trips a breaker or GFCI after repair: stop using it and call an electrician if the fault is in the outlet, not the cord.

title: Rewire a lamp cord end to end
mechanism_check: A lamp cord is two conductors (hot smooth side, neutral ribbed/stripe side) running from plug to socket; the socket shell is neutral, the center tab is hot.
The cord anchors at both ends with a strain-relief knot (underwriter's knot) so a tug pulls the knot, not the screws.
Polarity matters: hot must land on the brass screw/center tab, neutral on the silver screw/shell.
improvised_tools: New lamp cord (zip cord) cut to length — buy the cord, improvise the rest
Knife for stripping; flat screwdriver for the socket screws
A matchstick or toothpick to clear paint from old socket threads
steps: Unplug the lamp. Disassemble the socket and pull the old cord out, noting ribbed side to silver screw.
Cut the new cord to length. Tie an underwriter's knot: pass the cord up through the socket base, loop both conductors, pull tight.
Strip 1/2 inch, wrap the ribbed-side conductor clockwise around the silver screw, smooth side around brass.
Tighten both screws, tug to confirm the knot holds, reassemble the socket shell.
Plug in and test. If the lamp does not light, flip the bulb first, then re-check polarity before re-opening.
stop_conditions: Stop if the socket body is cracked, scorched, or the center tab is broken off — replace the socket, not just the cord.
Stop if the lamp is a vintage collectible with original wiring: rewiring changes its value; consult a specialist.
If the new cord shows heat damage or trips protection after install, call an electrician — the fault is upstream.

title: Replace a single-pole light switch
mechanism_check: A single-pole switch interrupts the hot leg only: two brass screws carry line-in and load-out, green screw bonds the ground.
Backstab terminals (push-in holes) are the failure-prone connection; side screws with a proper hook are the reliable one.
The switch yoke is held by two screws to the box; the wall plate is cosmetic.
improvised_tools: Phone photo of the old wiring before disconnecting — your reassembly map
Tape flags on the two hot wires to remember which was line vs load (matters for some smart switches later)
A butter knife or flat screwdriver to pry a stuck plate loose
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead with a lamp in the room's outlet or a non-contact tester if you own one.
Remove plate and yoke screws, pull the switch out gently, photograph the wiring.
Disconnect the old switch. Loop the two hot wires clockwise around the new switch's brass screws, tighten firmly.
Connect the bare/green ground to the green screw. Fold wires in, mount the yoke, replace the plate.
Restore power and test. If the switch does not work, re-check that both hots are secure before suspecting the fixture.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if you find three or more hot wires (three-way or multi-switch wiring) unless you have mapped it confidently.
Stop if the box is overcrowded, wires are scorched, or backstabs were melted — the circuit needs professional eyes.
Never work a switch with the breaker on 'to test as you go'. De-energize first, every time.

title: Replace a worn duplex outlet
mechanism_check: A duplex outlet has brass screws (hot), silver screws (neutral), green screw (ground); a break-off tab links the two halves for split circuits.
Loose grip on plugs means the internal contact springs are worn — the fix is replacement, not bending.
Multiple cable sets in the box mean the outlet also feeds downstream outlets; those wires must go back exactly.
improvised_tools: Tape flags to label line vs load wires when two cable sets share the box
Phone photo before disconnecting, per usual
A small flat screwdriver to release any backstabbed wires
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead with the lamp test. Remove plate and outlet screws, pull the outlet out.
Photograph everything. Note whether the break-off tab between the brass screws is intact or removed (split circuit).
Disconnect wires; wrap each clockwise around the matching screw on the new outlet (brass/black, silver/white, green/bare).
Match the break-off tab state of the old outlet exactly. Fold wires in, mount, plate on.
Restore power, test with a lamp, then plug something into both receptacles and tug gently — firm grip means a good job.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the break-off tab was removed and you cannot determine which circuit feeds which half.
Stop if you find scorched insulation, melted plastic, or a buzzing box with the power on — kill the breaker and call.
If the outlet is a GFCI or AFCI type, buy the same protection type; downgrading protection is not allowed.

title: Diagnose a breaker that keeps tripping
mechanism_check: Breakers trip on overload (too many amps for too long) or on short circuit/ground fault (huge instant current).
Trips immediately with everything unplugged = wiring fault. Trips after minutes with loads on = overload.
GFCI/AFCI breakers also trip on ground faults and arc faults — the breaker face usually says which.
improvised_tools: A written list of everything plugged into that circuit, made by walking room to room
Wattage math on a phone calculator: amps = watts / 120
A lamp as a single light load to test the bare circuit
steps: Flip the tripped breaker fully OFF, then ON. Unplug EVERYTHING on that circuit first.
If it holds with nothing plugged in, add loads back one at a time; the one that trips it is the culprit.
Add up the watts: a 15-amp circuit supports about 1440 watts continuous. If the total exceeds it, the circuit is simply overloaded.
If it trips with nothing plugged in, plug a lamp into each outlet on the circuit one by one — a dead outlet that trips it marks the fault location.
Spread heavy loads (space heaters, window AC, microwaves) across different circuits.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the breaker trips with everything unplugged — a wiring short or ground fault is live in the walls.
Stop if the breaker is hot, smells, buzzes, or shows scorch marks; kill it and call.
Never replace a breaker with a higher-amp one to 'stop the tripping' — the wire gauge sets the limit, not the breaker.

title: Fix an outlet where plugs fall out
mechanism_check: Plug grip comes from spring contacts inside each slot; they fatigue with age and heat cycles.
Loose contact means arcing risk: a plug that sags halfway out can spark under load.
Tension cannot be restored to a worn contact — replacement is the real fix; stopgaps buy time only.
improvised_tools: A power strip plugged into the worn outlet as a temporary safe host for plugs
Tape flags to mark which outlets are worn until replaced
Lamp test to confirm the outlet still makes solid electrical contact when a plug is held fully in
steps: Kill the breaker and verify dead before any work on the outlet itself.
Confirm the problem is the outlet, not the plug: test the same plug in a different outlet.
If the outlet is merely dusty, a careful blast of air can help — but do not bend the internal contacts back.
Replace the outlet (see electrical-009) as the real fix; schedule it, do not defer it.
Until replaced, route the load through a power strip seated firmly in the worn outlet, or use a different outlet.
stop_conditions: Stop using the outlet immediately if plugs feel warm, spark, or smell hot — kill the breaker and call an electrician.
Do not wedge, shim, or tape plugs into a worn outlet as a permanent fix.
If several outlets in the house are loose, call an electrician — the wiring era may need an audit.

title: Find which breaker feeds a circuit without a helper
mechanism_check: A breaker is a switch in series with the circuit: open it and everything downstream dies, nothing else.
Labeling is often wrong or missing, so the map must be built by test, not by reading.
Radios and lamps are the solo mapper's helpers: sound or light you can hear from the panel.
improvised_tools: A loud radio tuned to talk radio, plugged into the target outlet — you will hear it die from the panel
Phone on speaker call with yourself, or a video call aimed at the lamp, as a remote eye
Masking tape and marker to build the breaker map as you go
steps: Plug a loud radio (or lamp in view of a phone camera) into the outlet or room you want to map.
At the panel, flip breakers OFF one at a time, pausing a few seconds each, until the radio dies.
Flip that breaker back ON, confirm the radio returns, then label the breaker with tape.
Note everything else that died with it — same circuit — and label those rooms too.
Repeat for each room; keep the finished map taped inside the panel door.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if two breakers both seem to feed the same outlet — possible multi-wire fault.
Stop if breakers are unlabeled AND the panel is a recalled brand (Federal Pacific Stab-Lok, Zinsco); those need professional assessment.
Never leave a breaker half-tripped during mapping; flip fully OFF then fully ON.

title: Stop LED bulb flicker
mechanism_check: LEDs flicker when the dimmer is incompatible (old leading-edge dimmers chop power LEDs cannot smooth), when voltage sags, or when a loose connection arcs.
Flicker at full brightness with no dimmer points to a loose neutral or a failing bulb; flicker only when dimmed points to the dimmer.
One flickering LED among many on a circuit hints at the bulb; all flickering hints at the circuit or dimmer.
improvised_tools: A non-dimmable-free test: swap the suspect bulb into a non-dimmed lamp to isolate bulb vs dimmer
Your phone camera in slow-motion — it reveals flicker your eye misses
A second LED of a known-compatible brand as the control bulb
steps: First rule out the bulb: move it to a plain on/off lamp. If it still flickers, replace the bulb.
If it flickers only on the dimmer, confirm the dimmer is LED-rated (says LED/CFL on the face or box).
Replace an old incandescent-only dimmer with an LED-compatible dimmer (see electrical-014).
If all bulbs on the circuit flicker at full brightness, check for loose outlet/switch connections on that circuit.
Tighten any loose wire-nut splices or screw terminals you find de-energized.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if every light in the house flickers — the problem is the service feed or main neutral, not a bulb.
Stop if flicker comes with dimming of other lights when an appliance starts; that is a loose connection that needs professional tracing.
Never ignore flicker that smells of heat; kill the circuit and call.

title: Upgrade a switch to a dimmer
mechanism_check: A dimmer replaces the single-pole switch in the same box and wires identically (two hots + ground), but it dissipates heat and has a wattage rating.
Dimmer wattage rating must exceed the total bulb wattage on it — LED ratings are much lower than incandescent ratings on the same dimmer.
Some dimmers need a neutral wire in the box; check the box has a white neutral bundle before buying a neutral-requiring model.
improvised_tools: Phone photo of existing switch wiring as the reassembly map
Tape flags to mark line vs load if you plan smart-dimmer upgrades later
A calculator for the wattage sum: add every bulb the switch controls
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead. Remove the old switch, photograph the wiring.
Confirm the new dimmer is LED-compatible if any LED bulbs are on the circuit.
Connect the dimmer's two black leads to the two hot wires (order usually does not matter on single-pole), green to ground.
If the dimmer requires a neutral, join its white lead to the box's white neutral bundle with a wire nut.
Mount, restore power, and run the dimmer from low to high watching for flicker or buzzing.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if there is no neutral in the box and your dimmer requires one — do not bootleg ground as neutral.
Stop if the dimmer gets more than warm to the touch or buzzes loudly; it is overloaded or mismatched.
Never exceed the dimmer's wattage rating; if the load is too big, split the circuit or call an electrician.

title: Upgrade an outlet to a USB duplex outlet
mechanism_check: A USB outlet is a standard duplex with a low-voltage USB power supply built in; it wires to line voltage exactly like a normal outlet.
The built-in supply draws a small standby current forever — trivial per outlet, real across a house.
Deeper body than a plain outlet: shallow boxes may not fit it.
improvised_tools: A ruler or fingertip measure: the USB outlet needs roughly 2 inches of box depth
Tape flags for line vs load if the box has two cable sets
Phone charger as the post-install test load
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead. Pull the old outlet and photograph the wiring.
Check box depth: if the USB outlet cannot fold in without crushing wires, stop and use a box extender.
Wire it exactly like the old outlet: black to brass, white to silver, bare to green.
Mount, restore power, test both receptacles with a lamp and both USB ports with a phone.
Confirm the phone actually charges (not just 'connected') — a dead USB supply is a common defect.
stop_conditions: Stop if the box is too shallow and wires would be crushed; call an electrician for a deeper box or extender.
Stop if the USB ports are warm with nothing plugged in — defective unit, return it.
Call an electrician if the circuit is a split-wired or GFCI-protected outlet and you are unsure how to preserve the protection.

title: Replace a ceiling light fixture
mechanism_check: The fixture hangs from a mounting bracket screwed to the ceiling box; wires join box-to-fixture with wire nuts above the canopy.
Ceiling boxes on old fans or heavy fixtures may be fan-rated; a heavy new fixture needs that same support.
The fixture's black goes to the box black (hot), white to white, ground to the box ground and bracket.
improvised_tools: A second person or a loop of cord to hold the fixture while you wire — gravity is the enemy
Tape flags on the box wires before disconnecting the old fixture
Phone photo of the old connections
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead at the fixture with a lamp or tester.
Remove the old fixture's canopy, photograph, disconnect the wire nuts, and unscrew the mounting bracket.
Screw the new bracket to the ceiling box; confirm the box is snug and not cracked.
Hang the fixture from the bracket hook or a helper's hands; join black-black, white-white, ground-ground with wire nuts.
Tuck wires up, raise the canopy, install bulbs, restore power and test. Watch for wobble or sag.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the ceiling box is cracked, loose, or not rated for the fixture's weight.
Stop if you find aluminum wiring in the ceiling box — fixture connections need listed connectors and professional handling.
If the fixture is heavy (chandelier class) and the box is not fan-rated, call an electrician for proper support.

title: Balance a ceiling fan wobble
mechanism_check: Wobble comes from unbalanced blades, a loose downrod, or a mount that is not fan-rated; the motor itself is rarely the cause.
Blade weight kits work by adding small weights to find the heavy-light balance point across the blade set.
A wobbling mount saws at the ceiling box screws — the box must be fan-rated regardless of balance.
improvised_tools: Painter's tape and coins as improvised blade weights to find the balance point
A yardstick or tape measure to check blade tip height from the ceiling (all blades must match)
A screwdriver to check every downrod and bracket screw — the most common real fix
steps: Kill the fan's breaker before touching the mount. Tighten every visible screw: bracket, downrod, blade irons, blade screws.
Measure each blade tip's distance from the ceiling; gently bend misaligned blade irons until all tips match within 1/4 inch.
Run the fan on high. If it still wobbles, tape a coin to the top center of one blade and test; move it blade to blade to find the one that smooths it.
Replace the coin with a proper balancing-kit weight clipped at that blade's center.
Confirm the ceiling mount is a fan-rated box; a wobble that returns in weeks means the mount, not the blades.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the ceiling box is a plain light box or flexes — a fan needs a fan-rated box screwed to framing.
Stop if the downrod is bent or the motor housing is cracked; replace the fan.
If tightening and balancing do not fix a violent wobble, stop using the fan until the mount is professionally secured.

title: Replace a doorbell transformer
mechanism_check: The transformer steps 120V down to 16-24V for the chime; it usually hangs on a junction box near the panel, furnace, or in a closet.
Low-voltage side (thin bell wire to the chime) is safe to touch; the 120V primary side is not.
A dead chime with a warm transformer means the chime or button failed; a cold dead transformer with the breaker on means the transformer failed.
improvised_tools: A cheap multimeter if available — otherwise the chime itself is the tester
Tape flags to mark the two low-voltage bell wires before disconnecting
Phone photo of the primary-side wiring
steps: Kill the breaker feeding the transformer; verify the chime no longer gets power.
Label the two thin bell wires, disconnect them from the transformer's low-voltage screws.
Disconnect the 120V primary wires (black/white) from the transformer — photograph first.
Mount the new transformer (matching voltage: 16V or 24V as the chime requires), reconnect primary then bell wires.
Restore power; press the button. If the chime hums but does not ring, the chime mechanism — not the transformer — is next.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the transformer's 120V feed cannot be identified or de-energized with certainty.
Stop if the junction box is scorched or the transformer was hot enough to melt its case.
Never substitute a random wall-wart or undersized transformer; voltage and VA rating must match the chime.

title: Repair a broken holiday light string
mechanism_check: Mini-light strings are series-wired in sections: one dead bulb kills its section, a failed shunt keeps the rest lit dimly.
The fuse lives in the plug end — a blown fuse kills the whole string and is the first check.
Corroded sockets and loose bulbs are the usual section-killers, not broken wire.
improvised_tools: A known-good bulb pulled from a working string as the test bulb
Spare fuses from another string's plug (same rating) or the string's own spares
A pencil eraser to clean corroded socket contacts
steps: Unplug the string. Open the plug end and check the fuse; replace if the filament is broken.
Plug in and find the dead section. Starting at the first dark bulb, pull and reseat each bulb — loose bulbs are the top cause.
Swap the known-good bulb into each dark socket one at a time until the section lights; replace the culprit.
Clean green-corroded sockets with the eraser; if a socket is cracked, retire the string.
If half the string is dead and no bulb swap fixes it, the section wire is broken — retire the string.
stop_conditions: Stop and retire any string with cracked sockets, exposed copper, or melted plugs — repair is not worth the fire risk.
Never bypass the plug fuse or replace it with foil; the fuse is the string's only protection.
If the string trips a GFCI outdoors, stop using it — water has breached the insulation.
If a known-good string trips protection on a particular outlet, call an electrician — the outlet or circuit is at fault, not the lights.

title: Retrofit fluorescent tubes with LED tubes
mechanism_check: Fluorescent fixtures run tubes through a ballast; LED retrofit tubes either work with the ballast (plug-and-play) or need it bypassed (ballast-bypass/line-voltage).
Ballast-bypass is a permanent rewire of the fixture: line voltage goes straight to the tombstones, ballast removed from circuit.
Tombstones (the tube holders) must be non-shunted for single-ended ballast-bypass tubes.
improvised_tools: Phone photo of the ballast wiring before touching it
Wire nuts to cap the abandoned ballast leads after bypass
Tape flags to mark which tombstone wires were ballast-fed
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead. Decide: plug-and-play tubes (no rewiring, ballast stays) or ballast-bypass (rewire once, never buy ballasts again).
For ballast-bypass: disconnect and cap the ballast leads, wire line voltage directly to the tombstones per the tube maker's diagram.
Confirm tombstones are the type the tube requires (non-shunted for single-ended).
Install the LED tubes, restore power, and check for flicker or dark ends.
Label the fixture 'LED retrofit — no ballast' so the next person does not install fluorescent tubes in it.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the fixture wiring is brittle or the tombstones are cracked — the fixture needs replacement, not retrofit.
Stop if the LED maker's wiring diagram does not match your fixture's tombstone type.
Never install ballast-bypass tubes in a fixture still wired through the ballast — follow one method completely.

title: Size wire gauge and amp limits for cord projects
mechanism_check: Ampacity is the physics limit: thinner wire (higher gauge number) heats more under the same current.
Household rule of thumb: 14 AWG = 15A max, 12 AWG = 20A max, 16 AWG cords = 13A light duty, 18 AWG = lamp cords only.
Length matters: long runs add voltage drop, so size up one gauge for runs over 50 feet on heavy loads.
improvised_tools: Phone calculator: amps = watts / 120 for any appliance's nameplate
The cord's own jacket print — gauge is stamped on it; read it before trusting a guess
A tape measure for the run length
steps: Read the appliance's nameplate watts and compute amps (watts / 120).
Pick a cord rated above that amperage: 16 AWG for lamps and electronics, 14 AWG for power tools, 12 AWG for heavy loads.
For runs over 50 feet, go one gauge thicker to beat voltage drop.
Check the jacket stamp to confirm the gauge you bought matches the package claim.
Never daisy-chain cords to reach farther — one right-sized cord, or relocate the work.
stop_conditions: Stop if the load exceeds the cord's rating even at the thickest gauge you own — the circuit or the tool placement must change.
Anything permanently wired (new outlet, new circuit) is electrician work, not a cord project.
Stop using any cord that runs warm at the plug or along its length; it is undersized or damaged.

title: Build a lamp from a socket, cord, and plug
mechanism_check: A lamp is the simplest mains device: plug -> cord -> switch (optional) -> socket; hot to center tab, neutral to shell.
The socket shell must be the neutral side so the exposed screw threads are never hot.
Strain relief at both ends (knots or clamps) keeps tugs off the screw terminals.
improvised_tools: A bottle, jar, or driftwood piece as the lamp body — anything stable that the socket can mount to
Knife for stripping; screwdriver for terminals
An inline cord switch (cheap, no wiring skill needed) instead of a socket switch
steps: Choose a stable body and a way to mount the socket so it cannot tip: threaded rod through the body is the classic method.
Thread the cord through the body, tie strain-relief knots at the socket end.
Wire the socket: ribbed/neutral side to the silver screw (shell), smooth/hot side to the brass screw (center tab).
Wire the plug end: narrow prong = hot (smooth side), wide prong = neutral (ribbed side), green = ground if three-wire.
Assemble, install a bulb rated at or below the socket's wattage, plug in and test — then unplug and tug-test the knots.
stop_conditions: Stop if the lamp body is conductive metal and cannot be grounded — use a non-conductive body or a three-wire grounded build.
Stop if the socket is cracked or the wattage rating is unreadable; buy a new socket.
If the finished lamp trips protection or smells hot, unplug it and call an electrician before reusing.

title: Build an outage kit with honest battery runtime math
mechanism_check: Runtime is watt-hours divided by load watts: a 500Wh station running a 50W load lasts roughly 10 hours, minus inverter losses.
Prioritize: phones and medical devices first, then lights, then comfort; heating and cooling are generator-class loads.
Extension cords from a generator or station must be outdoor-rated and sized to the load.
improvised_tools: Phone calculator for the runtime math
A written load list: every device, its watts, and its priority rank
Car charger as the phone backup so the station serves lights and medical gear
steps: List what must stay powered in an outage with each item's watts from its nameplate.
Rank by priority: medical, communications, light, food safety, comfort — in that order.
Do the math: total watt-hours of your battery divided by the watts of the priority loads = honest runtime.
Size the kit to the math: if runtime falls short, cut loads — do not buy blind.
Store the kit charged, test it quarterly, and keep the load list taped to it.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician before wiring any generator into the house panel — backfeeding kills line workers.
Never run a fuel generator indoors or in a garage, even with the door open.
If medical devices are life-critical, confirm the backup plan with the device maker — improvised power is not a care plan.

title: Add a motion-sensor wall switch
mechanism_check: A motion-sensor switch replaces a single-pole switch and wires the same way, but it needs continuous standby power — some models need a neutral wire.
The sensor's range and timeout are adjustable; mis-aimed sensors are the top complaint, not wiring.
Bathroom fans and closets are the best first candidates; bedrooms are the worst (lights out while you read).
improvised_tools: Tape flags to mark the neutral bundle if present
Phone photo of the old wiring
Painter's tape to mask the sensor lens while aiming it
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead. Remove the old switch and photograph.
Check for a neutral bundle (white wires nutted together) if your sensor model requires one.
Wire the sensor: two hots to its line/load leads per the diagram, ground to green, neutral to neutral if required.
Mount, restore power, and set the timeout and sensitivity — start with 5 minutes and medium sensitivity.
Walk-test the coverage: adjust aim until it sees entry but not hallway traffic.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the box has no neutral and your model requires one — do not bootleg ground as neutral.
Stop if the sensor chatters or the controlled device is a fan motor the sensor is not rated for.
Never put a motion sensor on a circuit with medical or safety lighting that must never go dark.

title: Audit your home for overloaded circuits
mechanism_check: A 15A circuit safely carries about 1440 watts continuous (80% rule); 20A carries about 1920 watts.
The usual overloads: space heaters (1500W), window AC, microwaves, hair dryers — each nearly a full circuit alone.
Power strips do not add capacity; they only add outlets to the same limited circuit.
improvised_tools: Phone calculator and a notepad, room by room
The breaker map from electrical-012, or build it as you go
Wattage from appliance nameplates (stamped on the back or bottom)
steps: Map which outlets belong to each breaker (see electrical-012).
List everything plugged into each circuit with its watts; sum each circuit.
Flag any circuit over 1440W (15A) or 1920W (20A) — those are your overload risks.
Move the heavy portable loads (heaters, ACs) to different, lightly loaded circuits.
Recheck seasonally: winter heaters and summer ACs change the math.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if a circuit is overloaded and there is no lightly loaded circuit to move loads to — you may need a new circuit.
Stop if the audit reveals aluminum branch wiring or a Federal Pacific/Zinsco panel; both need professional assessment.
Never 'fix' an overload with a bigger breaker — the wire, not the breaker, sets the limit.

title: Run a space heater without burning the house down
mechanism_check: A 1500W heater draws 12.5 amps — nearly a full 15A circuit by itself; anything else on the circuit pushes it over.
Heaters fail by tipping over, by drying out nearby combustibles, and by melting undersized extension cords.
Tip-over switches and overheat cutoffs are the two safety features that matter; both must actually work.
improvised_tools: Your hand on the plug after 30 minutes — warm means the outlet or circuit is struggling
A tape measure for the 3-foot clearance zone around the heater
The breaker map to confirm the heater is alone on its circuit
steps: Plug the heater directly into a wall outlet — never into an extension cord or power strip.
Confirm nothing else heavy shares that circuit (see the audit in electrical-025).
Keep 3 feet of clearance on all sides: curtains, bedding, paper, furniture.
Test the tip-over switch: tilt the heater while off and listen for the click; replace the heater if it is silent.
After 30 minutes of use, feel the plug and outlet — they should be room temperature, not warm.
stop_conditions: Stop using the heater if the plug, outlet, or cord runs warm — kill the circuit and call an electrician.
Stop if the heater has no tip-over protection or a damaged cord; replace it.
If the breaker trips on the heater's circuit with nothing else plugged in, call an electrician — the circuit is compromised.

title: Run a temporary extension cord safely
mechanism_check: An extension cord is a temporary bridge, not wiring: it must be sized to the load, protected from damage, and removed when the job ends.
Outdoor use demands an outdoor-rated jacket (W stamped) and GFCI protection.
The failure points are the plug ends (heat) and anywhere the cord is pinched, walked on, or coiled tight under load.
improvised_tools: A doormat or cord cover to protect a cord crossing a walkway
Zip ties or hooks to keep the cord off the ground outdoors, out of puddles
Tape flags marking the cord's route so nobody trips or drives over it
steps: Size the cord to the load with the gauge rules (electrical-021): one right-sized cord, no daisy chains.
Run it where it will not be pinched by doors, walked on, or buried under rugs.
Outdoors: use an outdoor-rated cord plugged into a GFCI-protected outlet, elevated out of standing water.
Uncoil it fully under heavy load — a coiled cord traps its own heat.
Remove it when the job is done. If a 'temporary' cord has been there a month, it is wiring now — call an electrician for a real outlet.
stop_conditions: Stop using any cord that is warm, discolored, or smells hot.
Stop if the cord must cross where cars drive or doors slam — reroute or call an electrician for a permanent outlet.
Never run an extension cord through a wall, ceiling, or under carpet as a permanent installation.

title: Place and maintain smoke and CO detectors
mechanism_check: Smoke rises: detectors go on ceilings or high on walls, inside each bedroom, outside sleeping areas, and on every level.
CO is the silent killer from fuel-burning appliances; CO detectors go near bedrooms and fuel-burning equipment, not in the garage.
Hardwired units with battery backup stay linked so all sound together; a dead backup battery chirps to warn you.
improvised_tools: A broom handle to reach the test button on high ceilings
Canned air or a vacuum with a brush head to clear dust from the sensor chamber
Phone reminders for the twice-yearly battery swap and the 10-year replacement
steps: Walk the house: confirm a smoke detector inside each bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level including the basement.
Confirm CO detectors near bedrooms and any room with a furnace, water heater, or fireplace.
Press TEST on every unit — all hardwired units should sound together.
Vacuum each detector's vents; dust is the top cause of false alarms and dead sensors.
Replace any detector over 10 years old (date is stamped on the back) and any unit that fails the test button.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician (or the fire department's non-emergency line) if hardwired detectors fail to interconnect or the circuit misbehaves.
If a CO detector alarms, leave the house and call emergency services — do not investigate the source yourself.
Never disable a chirping detector by removing the battery without replacing it the same day.

title: Test outlet wiring with an improvised three-lamp check
mechanism_check: A proper outlet has hot on the narrow slot, neutral on the wide slot, ground on the round hole; swaps and missing grounds are the common faults.
A lamp with a polarized plug tests hot-vs-neutral orientation: it should light in both slots only when the plug orientation matches.
This improvised check finds dead and reversed outlets but cannot measure voltage or detect bootleg grounds — know its limits.
improvised_tools: A small lamp with a polarized plug (wide/narrow prongs) as the orientation tester
A three-prong plug with a known-good ground pin to feel for a solid ground-hole grip
Tape flags to mark suspect outlets for retesting with a real tester
steps: Verify the lamp works in a known-good outlet first.
Plug the lamp into the suspect outlet both ways. It should light normally with the plug fully seated.
Note any outlet where the lamp only lights when forced, or where the plug sits loose — flag for replacement.
Flag any outlet that fails the lamp test entirely for the dead-outlet diagnosis (electrical-001).
Treat every flagged outlet as suspect until verified with a real receptacle tester or by an electrician.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if multiple outlets show reversed or missing wiring — the circuit was miswired and needs professional correction.
Stop if you find outlets with no ground hole on a grounded system, or bootleg grounds — both need professional remediation.
This method never certifies an outlet as safe; it only screens for obvious faults. When in doubt, call.

title: Identify a switch-controlled outlet
mechanism_check: Many living rooms have one outlet half wired to a wall switch for lamps; the switch interrupts the hot leg to the top or bottom receptacle.
The giveaway: a wall switch that 'does nothing' usually controls an outlet.
Half-switched outlets often have the break-off tab removed between the brass screws.
improvised_tools: A lamp left plugged into the suspect outlet while you flip switches
Tape to mark which half is switched once found
A phone camera to photograph the tab state if you ever open it
steps: Plug a lamp into the outlet that 'has no power' and leave it there.
Flip every nearby wall switch one at a time, pausing between each.
When the lamp lights, you found it: mark the switch plate with tape ('controls outlet').
Test top and bottom receptacles separately — often only one half is switched.
If you replace that outlet later, preserve the tab state exactly or the switch control breaks.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the 'dead' outlet never responds to any switch and the breaker diagnosis finds no fault.
Do not rewire a switched outlet to be always-hot without understanding what the switch was for.
If the switch controlling it sparks or feels warm, kill the breaker and call an electrician.

title: Wire a combination switch-outlet device
mechanism_check: A combo device packs a switch and an outlet in one yoke; a break-off tab chooses whether the outlet is always-hot or switch-controlled.
It needs line hot, neutral, and ground in the box plus the load wire for whatever the switch controls.
Box fill gets tight fast: count wires against the box's stamped cubic-inch rating before committing.
improvised_tools: Tape flags for line, load, neutral, and ground — four roles, zero room for confusion
Phone photo of the old device wiring before disconnecting
A box-fill worksheet from the device instructions (or a quick cubic-inch count)
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead. Remove the old device, photograph, and label every wire's role.
Decide the tab state: tab intact = outlet always hot and switch independent; tab removed = switch controls the outlet.
Land the line hot on the device's line terminal, neutral on silver, ground on green, load wire on the switch terminal.
Check box fill: if wires are crushed to fit, stop — the box is too small for a combo.
Mount, restore power, and test all four states: switch on/off crossed with outlet live/dead as designed.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if box fill exceeds the stamped rating — a bigger box is a pro job.
Stop if the wiring does not match the device diagram (shared neutrals, no ground) — combo devices tolerate no improvisation.
If anything arcs, smokes, or trips on first power-up, kill the breaker and call.

title: Fish cable through a finished wall without a fish tape
mechanism_check: Inside a wall are studs every 16 inches, fire blocking in some walls, and insulation that grabs anything you push through.
The path must be planned stud-to-stud: find studs first, then cut access holes where the cable can actually travel.
Old-work boxes clamp to drywall; the cable must reach them with 6+ inches of slack inside the box.
improvised_tools: A straightened wire coat hanger as the probe and puller
A strong magnet on a string to catch a steel fish wire dropped from above
A stud finder, or the knock-and-listen method when you have none
steps: Map the studs and plan the route: vertical drops are easy, horizontal runs must dodge studs and blocking.
Cut a small probe hole and push the coat hanger through to feel for blocking, insulation, and existing wires.
Drop or push your pull wire through the clear path; use the magnet-on-string trick to catch it at the far hole.
Tape the cable to the pull wire with a smooth tapered wrap — no bulges that snag — and pull steadily.
Cut in old-work boxes at both ends, pull 8 inches of slack into each, and secure the cable within 12 inches of each box.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if you encounter existing wiring you cannot identify or must cross — one nicked cable is a fire.
Stop if fire blocking or a horizontal stud blocks the path; notching structure is beyond homeowner scope.
Never fish cable through a wall with live circuits you have not de-energized and verified dead.

title: Diagnose phantom (ghost) voltage readings
mechanism_check: Long parallel wire runs couple capacitively: a dead wire lying next to a live one picks up a 'phantom' voltage a high-impedance meter reads as real.
The tell: phantom voltage collapses under any real load (a lamp will not light) while real voltage holds.
Phantom readings cause false 'the circuit is still hot' scares — and false confidence if misread the other way.
improvised_tools: A lamp or other real load as the truth-teller: phantom voltage cannot light it
A low-impedance tester or solenoid 'wiggy' if available — immune to phantom readings
Tape flags to mark which conductors read phantom vs real
steps: With the circuit de-energized at the breaker, note which conductors still show voltage on a meter.
Connect a lamp across the suspect conductor and neutral: if it stays dark, the reading is phantom.
Trace which live circuit runs parallel to the dead one — shared conduit or bundled romex is the coupling path.
Confirm the breaker mapping is correct; a 'dead' wire that lights a lamp is NOT phantom — re-verify the panel.
Document the phantom pair on the breaker map so the next person is not fooled.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if a supposedly dead wire lights a lamp — your breaker map is wrong and something is miswired.
Stop if phantom readings appear on a circuit that should be isolated; shared neutrals across circuits need professional untangling.
Never dismiss a voltage reading as phantom without the lamp test proving it.

title: Inspect attic and crawlspace wiring for damage
mechanism_check: Damage hides where nobody looks: chewed insulation from rodents, junction boxes buried under blown insulation, splices made outside boxes.
Heat is the enemy in attics: insulation packed over recessed lights not rated for it (non-IC) is a fire setup.
Every splice must be in a covered, accessible box; an open splice in insulation is the classic attic fire starter.
improvised_tools: A bright headlamp — attics eat flashlight beams
Phone camera on a selfie stick to see behind ductwork and into tight bays
A wooden dowel to gently move insulation without stepping through the ceiling
steps: De-energize the circuits you will inspect closely; bring the headlamp and walk only on joists or decking.
Look for: chewed or bare conductors, open splice bundles, boxes buried under insulation, scorched wood near wiring.
Check recessed lights: confirm they are IC-rated if insulation touches them (label inside the housing).
Photograph every defect with its location; do not touch suspect splices beyond visual inspection.
Clear insulation back from non-IC fixtures and flag buried boxes for an electrician to expose and cover.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician for any open splice, chewed-through insulation, or scorched wood — do not repair these yourself.
Stop if you find knob-and-tube wiring buried in insulation; that combination is a known fire hazard needing professional remediation.
If the attic has vermiculite insulation (possible asbestos), stop the inspection and get it tested before disturbing anything.

title: Rebalance loads across two crowded breakers
mechanism_check: Two breakers feeding adjacent rooms often split loads badly: one idles while the other trips every winter.
Rebalancing means moving plug-in loads to the idle circuit's outlets — never moving breakers or rewiring the panel.
The constraint is the 80% continuous-load rule per circuit, measured honestly with nameplate watts.
improvised_tools: The home circuit audit from electrical-025 as the starting map
Phone calculator for the per-circuit watt totals
Long appliance cords or a relocated power strip to physically move loads
steps: Run the full circuit audit (electrical-025) and identify the overloaded circuit and the nearest lightly loaded one.
List which heavy loads are portable (heaters, dehumidifiers, chargers) versus fixed (hardwired lights).
Move portable loads to outlets on the idle circuit, keeping each circuit under 80% of its rating.
Live with the new arrangement for a week of typical use; note any trips.
If trips persist with honest math under 80%, the circuit has a fault — stop and call an electrician.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if rebalancing requires new outlets, new circuits, or any panel work — that is licensed work.
Stop if a circuit trips under 80% load after rebalancing; that is a failing breaker or wiring fault, not a load problem.
Never move a 240V appliance or hardwired load as part of a rebalance.

title: Add a photocell to a porch light
mechanism_check: A photocell is a light-sensitive switch wired in series with the fixture's hot leg: dark closes it, daylight opens it.
Screw-in photocell adapters need no wiring (they sit between bulb and socket); wired photocells splice into the hot lead.
The sensor must see sky, not the bulb it controls — a photocell staring at its own light will strobe all night.
improvised_tools: A screw-in photocell adapter as the zero-wiring option
Tape flags to mark the hot lead if you wire it inline
A piece of cardboard to simulate darkness during daytime testing
steps: Kill the breaker, verify dead. Choose: screw-in adapter (no wiring) or wired photocell (splice into the hot leg).
For the wired type: cut the fixture's hot lead, splice the photocell's black to line-hot, red to load-hot, white to neutral.
Aim the sensor eye away from the bulb and toward open sky.
Restore power in daylight: the light should stay OFF. Cover the eye with cardboard: it should turn ON within a minute.
Seal any new splices in the fixture box with wire nuts and confirm the canopy closes cleanly.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an electrician if the fixture box has no neutral for a wired photocell that requires one.
Stop if the light strobes or the photocell chatters — the sensor sees its own light and must be repositioned or shielded.
Never mount a photocell where it can fill with water; use a weather-rated unit outdoors.

title: Repair a frayed power-tool cord
mechanism_check: Tool cords fray at the strain relief where flexing concentrates; damage inside the jacket near the handle is common and invisible.
The safe repair is to cut back past all damage and re-terminate — either a new plug end or into the tool's own terminals.
Tape over a fray is never a repair: flexing re-opens it and the fault hides under the tape.
improvised_tools: A replacement plug end sized to the cord gauge
A knife to open the jacket and inspect how far the damage runs
Zip ties as temporary cord management so the repair point never flexes again
steps: Unplug the tool. Flex the cord along its length, feeling for soft spots, and cut the cord well above the highest damage.
Inspect the cut end: copper must be bright and the jacket intact. Cut higher until it is.
If enough cord remains, fit a new plug end (electrical-006). If the cord is now too short, open the tool and re-terminate at its internal terminals.
Reassemble with the strain relief properly seated — the repair must not flex at the new termination.
Test under load and flex the repair point while running; any stutter means redo it.
stop_conditions: Stop if damage runs into the tool's handle or housing — internal repair may need parts only the maker supplies.
Stop and replace the whole cord if the tool is double-insulated and the cord is molded in; field repair may void its safety listing.
If the tool trips protection after repair, stop using it and call an electrician — the fault is in the tool or the outlet.

title: Wire a low-voltage thermostat lead
mechanism_check: Thermostat wire is 24V low-voltage: safe to handle, but shorting R to C can blow the furnace's control fuse or transformer.
Standard colors: R = power, W = heat, Y = cool, G = fan, C = common; the C wire is what smart thermostats need.
The furnace end has the same terminals; both ends must match.
improvised_tools: Phone photos of both the old thermostat wiring and the furnace control board before touching either
Tape flags on each conductor labeled by terminal letter
A spare 3-amp automotive fuse as the sacrificial fuse if you blow the furnace fuse learning
steps: Kill power to the furnace at its switch/breaker — the 24V will not hurt you but a short will kill the control fuse.
Photograph the old thermostat's terminal letters and wire colors; do the same at the furnace board.
If adding a C wire, connect it to C at both ends; never repurpose G or steal power without understanding the board.
Land each wire on its matching letter at both ends; no stray strands bridging adjacent terminals.
Restore furnace power and run heat, cool, and fan modes to confirm each call works.
stop_conditions: Stop and call an HVAC tech if the furnace board has no C terminal and the thermostat needs one — add-a-wire adapters have limits.
Stop if you blow the control fuse twice; something is shorted and needs professional diagnosis.
Never work on the furnace's 120V supply side in this entry — that is electrician scope.

title: Mentor an apprentice through their first device replacement
mechanism_check: Apprentices learn the motor skill fast and the judgment slow: the failure mode is a helper who can wire an outlet but cannot tell when to stop.
The teaching mechanism is narration before action: every move gets said out loud before hands touch anything.
Mentoring fails when the journeyman does the work silently and the apprentice watches: watching is not practice.
improvised_tools: The three-sentence narration habit: say the circuit, the check, the move — 'breaker twelve is off, tester is dead, now I strip the hot'
A phone camera as the inspection tool: apprentice photographs every termination before the cover goes on
One spare device as a practice piece: wire and rewire it unpowered until the motions are smooth
steps: De-energize the circuit and verify dead yourself first; apprentice watches the verification, not just the flip.
Narrate the full plan before any cover plate comes off: what the device is, which wires land where, what you will check after.
Let the apprentice do the physical work while you narrate corrections — your hands stay in your pockets unless safety is at stake.
Have the apprentice photograph their terminations, then critique the photo together before re-energizing.
Re-energize and test together; if it fails, troubleshoot out loud so the apprentice sees the diagnostic path, not just the answer.
End with one question: 'what would you do differently next time' — their answer is the actual lesson.
stop_conditions: Stop the lesson and take over if the apprentice reaches past you toward a panel or device before verification is confirmed.
Stop if the apprentice is rushing to look competent — speed is a stop sign, not a virtue; slow them or end the session.
Call a licensed electrician for anything past homeowner scope no matter who is holding the screwdriver; the apprentice's lesson that day is 'when to call.'

title: Estimate a small job: honest materials and labor math
mechanism_check: Estimates fail two ways: materials priced from memory (wrong) and labor guessed (optimistic). Both come from skipping the walkthrough.
The mechanism is counting what you can touch: every device, every box, every foot of cable on the plan before any number is written.
Labor math is hours times your rate plus a fudge factor you admit to yourself: first-timers under-estimate by roughly double.
improvised_tools: Phone photos of the panel and every room: the estimate lives in the pictures, not in memory
A notes-app template: devices, wire footage, breakers, consumables, hours, contingency — same order every job
A receipt-envelope habit: keep one job's actual costs and compare against the estimate after
steps: Walk the job with the homeowner: count every device, box, fixture, and run; photograph the panel and each room.
List materials from the count using your last real purchase prices, not catalog guesses; add wire footage plus 20% waste.
Estimate labor hours from your slowest past job of the same type, not your fastest — then add one hour of contingency per day.
Write the total with materials and labor as separate lines; never hide one inside the other.
Present the number, shut up, and let the homeowner react — defending an honest estimate is better than revising a dishonest one.
After the job, compare actual costs to the estimate in your receipt envelope and adjust your next estimate's fudge factor.
stop_conditions: Stop and call a licensed electrician for the estimate if the job touches the panel, the service feed, or anything the homeowner cannot legally have you do.
Stop bidding if you cannot name every device and run from your walkthrough photos — re-walk instead of guessing.
Never cut the estimate by deleting safety steps (no permits where required, no skipped verification); the bid that drops safety is a bid you walk away from.

title: Build the de-energize-first habit until it is automatic
mechanism_check: Safety habits fail because they are decisions: every decision is a chance to choose wrong under time pressure. Habits replace decisions.
The mechanism is the trigger-action link: 'I am about to touch a device' must fire 'breaker off, verify dead' before any hand moves.
The habit is proven by the awkward case: you still verify dead on the second visit to the same circuit, because yesterday's verification is today's assumption.
improvised_tools: A non-contact tester on your belt, not in the truck: the check has to be physically easier than skipping it
The touch rule: back of the hand never goes near a conductor until the tester has said dead twice — test the tester on a live circuit first, then on the work circuit
A piece of tape on the panel: write the circuit number while it is off so the habit leaves a trace
steps: Before touching any device, say the circuit number out loud — naming it engages the part of your brain that skips shortcuts.
Flip the breaker fully OFF, then test your tester on a known-live outlet so you know the tester works.
Test the device you are about to touch; test hot-to-ground and hot-to-neutral, not just one.
Tape or lock the breaker and put your name on the tape — even if you are the only one home.
Only then remove the cover plate; if anything interrupts you, re-verify before your hands go back in.
When finished, re-energize and test the device works — the habit closes the loop it opened.
stop_conditions: Stop if you cannot positively identify the breaker for the circuit — flip the main only as a last resort, and call an electrician if the panel is unmarked and the load cannot wait.
Stop if the tester is behaving oddly or its battery is questionable — treat 'tester might be lying' as 'circuit is live.'
Call a licensed electrician the moment the work would require opening the panel or working near the service feed; no habit makes that safe for homeowner scope.

title: Read a breaker panel schedule like a map
mechanism_check: An unlabeled panel is a memory test every job: the schedule turns 'I think it is number nine' into written fact.
The mechanism is the two-column truth: left column is the breaker's position, right column is everything it feeds — both written at the panel, not in a drawer.
Schedules drift: circuits get reworked and the paper lies. The maintenance habit is re-verifying one circuit per visit.
improvised_tools: A printed or handwritten schedule card taped inside the panel door — paper beats a phone photo when the power is out
A circuit-directory update ritual: change the schedule the day you change the wiring, never 'later'
The odd-one-out check: any double-tapped breaker or mystery blank gets flagged, not ignored
steps: De-energize nothing yet: first transcribe what the panel already says, position by position, including blanks and double-taps.
Using the lamp/radio method from electrical-012, verify each breaker feeds what the schedule claims — correct the card as you go.
Note the amperage of each breaker next to its loads; flag any circuit whose known loads look heavy for its rating.
Write the finished schedule in plain words ('kitchen outlets, east wall') not codes; tape it inside the panel door.
Photograph the final card for your records so a faded original is never the only copy.
Each future job: re-verify the one circuit you are touching and initial the card's margin — the map stays true one circuit at a time.
stop_conditions: Stop and call a licensed electrician if you find scorched bus bars, a burning smell in the panel, or breakers that will not reset — reading a schedule never involves opening the panel interior.
Stop if double-tapped breakers or mystery circuits make the map unreliable: mark them UNKNOWN and get a pro, do not guess.
Never relabel a breaker by flipping it and assuming — verify with a load test every time, even when you are 'sure.'

title: Torque terminations to spec and stop over-tightening
mechanism_check: Loose terminations arc and start fires; over-torqued terminations crack devices and strip threads. The right torque is a number, not a feeling.
The mechanism is the manufacturer's in-lb rating: receptacles and breakers both print it, and a torque screwdriver turns 'tight enough' into verifiable.
Career-grade work is inspectable work: torqued connections are the difference between 'it works' and 'it is provably safe.'
improvised_tools: A torque screwdriver or torque wrench adapter — the single tool that separates apprentice work from journeyman work
The spec habit: read the in-lb number off the device before the first screw, not after
A tug test after torquing: pull each conductor firmly to confirm it is captured, not just pressed
steps: De-energize the circuit, verify dead, and remove the device cover.
Read the torque spec printed on the device or in its instructions; set the torque driver to that value.
Strip to the device's gauge mark, form the wire so it sits fully under the screw or clamp plate without insulation caught.
Drive each terminal to the torque setting — the tool clicks or slips, and you stop; no extra quarter-turn 'for luck.'
Tug-test every conductor, then photograph the finished terminations for your records.
Re-energize, test the device under load, and recheck warmth at the device after a few minutes of load.
stop_conditions: Stop if a terminal will not hold torque — stripped threads or cracked device bodies get replaced, never shimmed or epoxied.
Stop and call a licensed electrician if the conductors are aluminum and you are not trained and tooled for AL terminations (anti-oxidant, CO/ALR devices).
Call an electrician if you find melted insulation or discolored terminals — that connection already failed once; a pro should see why.

title: Combine rough-in and trim-out into one two-pass workflow
mechanism_check: Two trips to the same room waste half a day: rough-in work (boxes, cable, mounting) and trim-out (devices, fixtures) can be planned as one job with two passes instead of two jobs.
The mechanism is the room checklist: every device the room needs is decided on paper before pass one, so pass two is pure assembly with no decisions left.
The combination fails when trim-out surprises appear (wrong box depth, missing neutral) — the fix is a pass-one verification step that proves each box ready before you leave.
improvised_tools: A per-room sheet: box count, device type, fixture type, special notes — one page per room, filled before any cable is cut
The pass-one exit test: tug every cable, confirm box depth and fill, photograph each open box
A trim-out tote packed per room from the sheet: devices, plates, bulbs, wire nuts — nothing fetched mid-pass
steps: Walk every room and fill the per-room sheet: devices, fixtures, switches, box depths, any smart-device neutral requirements.
Pass one (rough-in): set boxes, run and secure cable, leave generous conductor length; photograph every open box.
Run the pass-one exit test on each box: depth right, cable secured, enough conductor, correct cable type — fix now, not later.
Pack the trim-out tote per room directly from the sheet; stage totes so pass two is a single walk.
Pass two (trim-out): de-energize each circuit, verify dead, install devices and fixtures room by room; no mid-pass supply runs.
Final: energize room by room, test every device, and file the room sheets — they are the as-built record for the next job.
stop_conditions: Stop and call a licensed electrician if pass one reveals knob-and-tube, ungrounded runs, or panel capacity problems — the two-pass plan does not cover remediation.
Stop if the pass-one exit test finds a box you cannot make compliant (fill, depth, support) — re-plan that room instead of burying the problem behind a device.
Never energize to 'test early' mid-trim-out: de-energize-first applies to every room, every pass, no exceptions.

title: Level up: learn conduit bending from one hand bender
mechanism_check: Conduit bending is the craft's visible signature: straight runs with clean bends signal competence before a single wire is pulled.
The mechanism is take-up and shrink math: every bend consumes a fixed amount of conduit, and the bender's marks encode it — learn the marks, not the formulas, to start.
The beginner failure is the scrap pile: practice on short cutoffs, not on the run, until the first 90 lands within a quarter inch of the mark.
improvised_tools: One hand bender matched to your conduit size (half-inch EMT to start) — one bender learned deeply beats three borrowed
A tape measure and a Sharpie: measure to the back of the 90, mark clearly, bend once
A cutoff practice bundle: ten short pieces of conduit for the week's drills, not the job's material
steps: Learn the bender's star and arrow marks on scrap: bend a 90, measure the take-up, and write your bender's number on its handle.
Drill 90s on cutoff pieces until five in a row land within a quarter inch of the mark.
Drill offsets (two 45s) next: measure the obstruction depth, mark both bends, check the conduit clears.
Only then bend on the job: measure twice, mark once, bend once — and cut the conduit after the bend, not before.
Mount with straps per code spacing; a bent run that is not secured is not finished.
Log your take-up numbers per bender and conduit size — that note card is your personal bending chart.
stop_conditions: Stop if the bender is kinking the conduit — wrong shoe size or too-fast bend; get guidance before you waste the run.
Stop and call a licensed electrician if the run enters a panel or crosses into work past homeowner scope — bent conduit does not authorize live-panel work.
Never heat EMT to bend it: hand benders cold-bend for a reason; heated conduit loses its listing and its strength.

title: Run lockout/tagout as a two-person team
mechanism_check: Lockout/tagout fails on crews when one person flips the breaker and everyone assumes it stays flipped. The mechanism is personal locks: each worker's lock is their own life, never shared, never borrowed.
The coordination challenge is handoffs: on a multi-person job, the last lock removed re-energizes, so the removal order is the safety plan.
The failure mode is trust without verification: 'I watched him lock it' is not a lock on the hasp — only your lock counts for you.
improvised_tools: A hasp and two padlocks — one lock per worker, keyed differently; the hasp is the cheapest life insurance on the truck
Tags with name, date, and reason: the tag speaks when the worker is in the attic and cannot
The buddy-check ritual: before hands go in, each worker verifies the other is locked on — out loud, every time
steps: Both workers identify the circuit together and agree on the breaker — no unilateral lockouts.
Worker one flips the breaker OFF, both verify dead with a tested tester, and worker one locks and tags the hasp.
Worker two adds their own lock and tag to the same hasp — two locks, two keys, neither can energize alone.
Buddy-check out loud: 'I am locked, you are locked, the circuit is dead' — said, not assumed.
Work proceeds; if anyone leaves the job, their lock stays until they return and remove it themselves.
Re-energize only after both locks are removed by their owners, in reverse order, with a final all-clear call.
stop_conditions: Stop the job if anyone is pressured to remove another person's lock or 'just flip it real quick' — that is the stop-work line, full stop.
Stop and call a licensed electrician if the panel cannot accept a lock or hasp — no lock means no crew work, improvised blocks do not count.
Escalate to the job owner if a lock's key is lost: the lock gets cut only with everyone's eyes on and the circuit re-verified dead after.

title: Coordinate a two-person wire pull through a long run
mechanism_check: A long pull binds when the feeder pushes blind and the puller yanks hard: the mechanism is rhythm — steady feed, steady pull, constant communication.
The coordination challenge is that the two workers cannot see each other: the feeder feels jams the puller cannot, and the puller feels tension the feeder cannot.
Pulls fail from force, not friction: a hard yank kinks the cable in the wall; a patient re-feed clears most binds in seconds.
improvised_tools: A two-tap signal system when radios are absent: two taps on the conduit means 'feed,' three means 'stop' — agreed before the pull starts
Lubricant for long or multi-bend pulls: soap or purpose-made lube on the cable head, never petroleum on NM jacket
The feeder's chair: a seated, braced position so feeding is arms, not back — exhaustion causes the hard yanks that kink cable
steps: Agree on signals (taps, shouts, or radios) and the stop word before anyone pulls — rehearse it once.
Feeder stages the cable so it feeds straight into the box with no kinks; puller attaches the head and confirms the signal.
Puller pulls in a steady rhythm; feeder feeds slightly ahead of the pull so the cable never goes taut at the box.
At the first sign of a bind, puller stops on signal — never yanks; feeder backs the cable out six inches and re-feeds while puller resumes gently.
Feeder calls out footage so the puller knows how much remains; the last ten feet go slowest.
After the pull, both inspect the cable jacket for gouges before any termination — a damaged pull gets re-pulled, not hidden.
stop_conditions: Stop the pull if the cable head separates in the wall — do not fish it with power tools blind; reassess or call an electrician.
Stop if anyone is tempted to lube and yank through a bind that has resisted three gentle tries — a jammed run may have a damaged box or staple; open the wall or call a pro.
Call a licensed electrician if the pull route turns out to cross the service entrance or main panel interior.

title: Improvise together when the parts run comes up wrong
mechanism_check: Crews lose half a day to wrong parts: the mechanism is the runner's information — a runner with a photo and a device in hand returns correct, a runner with a description returns hopeful.
The coordination challenge is splitting the crew without stalling it: one person runs, the rest pivot to work that needs no parts.
The failure mode is the substitute trap: an almost-right part installed 'temporarily' becomes permanent and wrong.
improvised_tools: The parts photo: the old or failed device, its ratings label, and the box it came from — photographed, sent to the runner
A pivot list kept per job: tasks needing no parts (clean-up, labeling, panel schedule updates, prep) that fill any wait
The no-substitute rule, stated at the job start: 'if the exact part is not on the truck, we pivot — we do not improvise the part'
steps: When the wrong part surfaces, stop that task immediately — do not 'make it work.'
Photograph the needed part, its ratings, and the mating hardware; text it to the runner with the store aisle if known.
The runner takes the failed device itself when possible — matching in hand beats matching from memory.
While the runner is out, the crew works the pivot list: no idle hands, no rushed improvisation.
On return, verify the part against the photo and the ratings label before unwrapping — wrong-twice costs the day.
Log the mix-up: what was ordered, what arrived, why — the next job's order list improves from this one.
stop_conditions: Stop and call a licensed electrician if the correct part is unavailable and the circuit cannot stay safely de-energized until it is — no improvised substitutions on safety-critical parts.
Stop if anyone proposes a cross-rated substitute (wrong amperage, wrong voltage, unlisted device) — the no-substitute rule has no exceptions.
Escalate to the homeowner if the delay pushes past the day: an honest schedule update beats a corner cut.

title: Run the five-minute teach-back huddle at day's end
mechanism_check: Skills evaporate between jobs unless they are named: the mechanism is the teach-back — the person who did the work explains what they did, and explaining is what makes it stick.
The coordination challenge is the clock: crews skip the huddle when tired, which is exactly when the day's mistakes go unrecorded.
Five minutes works because it is bounded: one lesson, one question, one fix — longer huddles become meetings and die.
improvised_tools: The huddle spot: same place, same time, tools down — ritual location makes the habit survive bad days
The three prompts, always in order: 'what did you learn,' 'what almost went wrong,' 'what do we change tomorrow'
A pocket notebook per crew member: each person writes their one lesson before leaving — paper beats memory
steps: Call the huddle at the same time daily: tools down, circle up, five minutes on the clock.
Each person answers 'what did you learn today' in one sentence — the newest person goes first so seniors do not set the ceiling.
Each person answers 'what almost went wrong' — near-misses are named without blame; the point is the lesson, not the fault.
The crew picks one change for tomorrow from the near-misses; the lead writes it on the job board or a shared note.
Everyone writes their own one-line lesson in their notebook before leaving.
Next morning's first act: read yesterday's change aloud — the loop closes or it was theater.
stop_conditions: Stop the huddle if it turns into blame or jokes at someone's expense — the lead ends it and restarts the ritual clean tomorrow.
Escalate any near-miss that involved a shock, a spark, or a tripped main: the huddle records it, but a licensed electrician reviews the cause before work resumes.
If the same near-miss repeats three days running, stop treating it as a lesson and treat it as a process failure — change the process, not the pep talk.

title: Call the crew stop-work play when something smokes mid-job
mechanism_check: Panic is the mechanism that hurts people: smoke triggers freeze or flailing, and a crew without a drilled play does whichever comes first.
The coordination challenge is authority: someone must say 'stop' and everyone must obey instantly — which only works if the word and the response are agreed beforehand.
The play succeeds when de-energizing and distance happen before diagnosis: the first sixty seconds are about safety, not answers.
improvised_tools: The stop word: one agreed word ('STOP-WORK') that halts all hands instantly — chosen at the job start, used by anyone, obeyed by everyone
The de-energize sprint: one person owns the path to the panel and nothing else when the word is called
A rally point outside the work area: everyone knows where to regroup so a headcount is possible
steps: Anyone calls the stop word at the first sign of smoke, spark, or burning smell — no one needs permission and no one argues.
The panel person moves: breaker for the circuit OFF immediately; if the source is unclear or the panel is involved, the main goes OFF.
Everyone steps back to the rally point; the lead does a headcount — nobody re-enters until the count is right.
Only after distance and de-energizing: assess from afar — where was the smoke, is it spreading, is anyone hurt.
If there is fire or spreading smoke, evacuate and call emergency services — tools and schedule are abandoned, not debated.
After the all-clear, nothing re-energizes until the cause is found; if the cause is not obvious and safe, a licensed electrician finds it.
stop_conditions: Stop the job for the day if the stop word was called and the cause is not fully understood — 'probably fine' is how the second call happens.
Call a licensed electrician whenever the smoke came from inside a panel, a breaker, or wiring you did not install — no crew diagnoses that in the field.
